Further, they suggest increased transparency with regards to the possibility that these events may not be ripples but rather high frequency oscillatory events that reflect spiking activity. Further suggestions for revisions are below.

Essential revisions:

1) The results as-is do not support the claim that ripples are discrete events. The reviewers suggest the authors include additional analyses to demonstrate that ripples are discrete events or instead remove these claims and report on the findings/characterization of these high frequency events and their relationship to spiking activity and memory.

2) To unambiguously demonstrate that ripples are discrete events, the authors could generate a plot of the distribution of detection features, such as binned ripple power of the LFP electrodes, which would presumably need to be bimodal. If, as would be expected from the rodent literature and the results of this study, the authors instead observe a long-tailed distribution, the data would clearly demonstrate that these are not discrete events. If so, rather than fighting to prove the "discrete" nature of ripples, it would be more productive to embrace the variability in event sizes and take a more "signal detection" -style approach to this challenge. In line with this approach, methods have been developed which first model the noise of the signal and use this to set a somewhat less arbitrary threshold for event detection (Yu et al., eLife 2017), which demonstrate that events far smaller than would have been detected using traditional thresholds are likely to be biologically meaningful.

3) In addition to using more sensitive detection methods, the authors can ask how results, such as phase coupling or spiking modulation, vary over different sizes of events, and perhaps identify features that can inform less arbitrary detection thresholds for future work. Further, it would be extremely useful to see how the different sizes of LFP events are differentially detectable/reflected in the iEEG signal. For instance, it would be informative to know what proportion of events detected in the iEEG coincide with events in the LFP, and how this varies over a range of detection thresholds applied to each type of recording.

4) The title of Figure 1 would suggest that the authors will demonstrate the discrete nature of ripple events, however, the examples and analyses in this figure do not address this question. Unless the authors can show that there are clearly bimodal distributions underlying ripple events, It would be preferable to set aside the "discrete" claim throughout the manuscript and instead use this figure to address the detection methodology and show the characteristics of ripples in iEEG and LFP over a range of detection thresholds.

5) Also regarding Figure 1, it is unclear how much of the findings showing differential engagement of ripples/HFA on correct vs incorrect retrievals are re-prints of previously published findings, replication of previous findings with new or additional data, or new findings. Please specify.

6) An illustration like Figure 2A with much more detail and quantification would be extremely helpful for developing a better intuition for how to evaluate the resultant data. For instance, is a single iEEG contact consistently directly above, and exactly the same size as, the MEA, as suggested by Figure 2A? Where do the MEA electrode tips tend to lie in relation to cortical layers? Additionally, it would be critical to specify exactly how the spatial layout of electrodes, and the brain areas targeted, varied over the individual patients.

7) Regarding figures 2 and 3, more analyses of how often events detected in the iEEG would coincide with events detected in the LFP and/or cross-correlograms of the time of peak power for each event would be useful instead or in addition to the current approach of applying event detection in one data type and then plotting the continuous measure from the other datatype. In addition, it would be useful if the authors reported, in the text, the amount of variance for each relationship, not just whether a regression is significant. For example, in Figure 2c, the signal from a local LFP electrode captures ~36% of the variance in spiking rate, while the signal from the iEEG electrode captures ~1.4% of the variance. The authors are making claims about iEEG reflecting the LFP or spiking, and it's important that these claims be quantified with the strengths of the relationships, not just whether they are significant or not.

8) Regarding figures 2-4, would it be possible to glean more statistical power by capturing the variability of events within each patient as well as the variability across patients by using linear mixed-effects models for the summary statistics such as those shown in Figure 2D, F, H, etc? These models generally provide a much better way to describe relationships when large data samples have been collected from multiple subjects.

9) With regards to the quantification of the strengths of the relationships, it might be helpful if the authors quantified the same relationships across the spatial extent of the MEA. That might allow them to estimate the fall-off of predictability with distance on short length scales, which would give them a first order prediction of what they might see on the larger scales of the distances from the iEEG contacts to the MEA.

10) Additional raw data examples (similar to Figure 2B or 4A) including the full LFP band signal from several MEA sites (not only the 80-120Hz filtered traces) would be useful to add into the supplementary figures. In particular, it would be informative to be able to compare the full LFP signal to the full 1-200Hz iEEG trace.

11) In the experiment, authors assigned a randomly correct response time to 'pass' trials and categorized these 'pass' trials as incorrect. The randomly assigned response time smear out the effect of vocal-locked responses of incorrect trials. It might be one reason underlying the difference between incorrect and correct trials. Authors perhaps can include only the 'intrusive' trials as incorrect trials and see how the result look like.

12) The authors found that the amplitude of ripple events reflected the local spiking activities which was consistent with results from a study by Logothetis et al. showing that the gamma activity of LFP is related with local single unit activities. How could the authors distinguish the difference between their ripple activity and Logothetis's gamma activity?

13) What is the difference between iEEG ripples and LFP ripples? Do they differ in amplitude? Do they come from the same origin? I suggest adding details as to how they differ.

14) The micro arrays were placed within the expected resection area. I understand the potential damage to the brain if it is placed in a healthy area. However, how do the authors think it affects the results? It perhaps would be difficult to perform any control analyses given the current dataset. Maybe the authors can pay some lines in the discussion.

15) About the criterion of defining ripple events: In the methods part of 493-495, the criterion was already liberal compared to rodent studies. The authors however took an even more liberal criterion in another analysis (line 503-507). Perhaps the authors should call these events gamma bursts instead of ripples.

16) When performing the pairwise phase consistency analysis, they assigned the maximum PPC computed over the duration of each iEEG ripples as the LFP 80-120 Hz PPC for that iEEG ripple. It seems that they have a hypothesis that the PPC of LFP 80-120Hz which does not satisfy as ripple criterions is comparable with PPC of LFP ripples. I however did not find the supporting data.

17) I think the authors should be more transparent about the possibility that a portion of their defined "ripple" events may not in fact be ripples but high frequency activity events that relate to spiking activity. I suggest renaming these events to "ripple-like" and adding relevant discussion on this topic.

18) While the authors acknowledge the limitation of their ripple detection methods, they go on to argue in their conclusions that their results provide evidence that human ripple activity are thus more variable and exist on a "continuum of amplitudes and scales". I was not convinced by this argument since it is also possible that many of these events are simply not ripples and rather could be high frequency events that reflect spiking activity.

19) The statement "neural activity in the human cortex is organized into dynamic, discrete packets of information" seems out of place and not directly related to what the study is attempting to show. I suggest removing it or rephrasing.

20) Very difficult to evaluate Figure 2 since the legend is an exact copy from figure 1. Please revise.

21) It would be nice if the authors can include how many "ripple" events overlapped with IED events.

[Editors' note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for submitting your article "Ripples reflect a spectrum of synchronous spiking activity in human anterior temporal lobe" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Joshua Gold as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) Claims that ripples reflect discrete events should be removed or further analyses should be completed and results included to support this conclusion.

2) Simultaneous recording of LFP and iEEG, and the associated findings are a major strength of the study and should be further highlighted throughout the manuscript.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The manuscript is much improved and the authors have done a nice job responding to reviewer concerns. The added analyses, including the investigation of medial temporal and anterior temporal ripples as well as LFP-IEEG ripples are a nice addition. Further the authors have added important language acknowledging the variability in features of human ripples as reported and potential differences between those found in rodents. I think the community would benefit from the revised manuscript and recommend publication.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

In their revised manuscript, Tong et al. make a solid case to link neural spiking with patterns of oscillatory activity recorded at the local field potential and intracranial EEG levels. They have softened their claims about discrete packets of activity, and instead focus on establishing relationships between the different neural recording approaches over a range of event sizes and detection thresholds. We have two major suggestions to improve the clarity of their manuscript.

First, while the authors have moved away from focusing on whether ripples can be considered discrete events, this claim still comes up in several prominent places (including in the titles of their first Results section and figure) and continues to cause confusion. The authors now claim equally or more strongly that ripples exist on a continuum, which seems contradictory and incompatible with the claim of discreteness. The claim of discreteness is not central to the important message that these events are meaningful, that they can be detected by the various recording modalities, and that they reflect underlying neural spiking activity. Given this, it would likely be best if the authors simply remove all claims of discreteness. However, we also appreciate that the authors have included distributions of ripple features and can show that these can appear bimodal. If the authors truly want to demonstrate discreteness, further explanation of Figure 2-Supplement 4 is needed as well as more prominent positioning of this result in a main figure and further analysis of the events detected by this method. Indeed, if this bimodality is truly robust, then an improved detection method would use the dip in the distribution as the detection threshold for each session/subject for all subsequent analysis. Further, this detection approach could/should then be compared to the more traditional thresholds.

Second, the authors note several times throughout the manuscript that a particular challenge in understanding ripples is the range and variety of detection methods used (for instance, lines 34-36). This is absolutely true, but a perhaps even more critical challenge is the difficulty of comparing ripples detected by the two major recording techniques – LFP for rodent work and iEEG for human work. Critically, the authors are particularly well-positioned to shed light and improve our understanding of how the LFP and iEEG signals relate to each other, and they should incorporate this point as a major strength of their study throughout their manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Thanks for authors' efforts on the revised manuscript. Questions proposed during the first round were carefully taken care of by authors. The manuscript was also properly revised.

results.result: The study involved 21 participants with drug-resistant epilepsy who underwent surgical implantation of intracranial recording electrodes. In six participants, microelectrode arrays (MEAs) were additionally implanted in the anterior temporal lobe for research purposes. The study was conducted at the NIH Clinical Center with IRB approval and informed consent.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C102, and C103 provide clear methodological details about participant recruitment, surgical procedures, and ethical approvals. These are standard methodological claims that are well-documented and internally consistent.

results.result: The study demonstrates that 80-120 Hz ripple oscillations contribute to broadband high-frequency activity in the human temporal cortex. These ripples exist on a spectrum of amplitudes and durations that are related to underlying neuronal spiking activity. Macro-scale iEEG ripples are related to the number and synchrony of micro-scale LFP ripples, which in turn are related to neuronal spiking synchrony.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7, C65, and C66 represent the core findings of the manuscript and are supported by converging evidence from multiple spatial scales (iEEG, LFP, and single-unit recordings). The data in Figures 1-4 provide strong empirical support for these conclusions, including correlational analyses, control analyses removing ripples, and direct measurements of spiking activity.

results.result: During memory retrieval, transient increases in high-frequency activity (70-200 Hz) correspond to discrete 80-120 Hz ripple events. Both HFA and ripple rates increase prior to vocalization during successful memory retrieval compared to unsuccessful retrieval, with similar anatomical distributions. The correlation between HFA and ripple rate is particularly strong in the medial temporal lobe (r=0.60, p=0.00072) and anterior temporal lobe (r=0.23, p=0.026).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are well-supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and associated statistical analyses. The correspondence between HFA and ripple events is demonstrated both at the single-trial level and across participants, with appropriate statistical tests and anatomical specificity.

results.result: The correlation between HFA and ripple rate is consistent across participants during both baseline (r=0.085±0.018) and retrieval (r=0.093±0.020) periods, with both significantly greater than zero (p<1×10⁻⁶). The relationship is similar between baseline and retrieval (p=0.083) but stronger during correct compared to incorrect retrieval (p=0.013).
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (t-tests) with clear reporting of effect sizes and p-values. The finding that the HFA-ripple relationship is modulated by memory performance adds behavioral relevance to the neural observations.

results.result: Removing discrete 80-120 Hz ripples from the signal eliminates the difference in 70-200 Hz power between correct and incorrect memory retrieval. After ripple removal, the correlation between ripple rate differences and HFA differences is no longer significant (r=-0.042, p=0.270). No significant correlation was found between HFA and 120-200 Hz ripple rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 describe a critical control analysis that demonstrates the specific contribution of 80-120 Hz ripples to broadband HFA. The control analysis is well-designed and the results are clearly reported with appropriate statistics. The lack of correlation with 120-200 Hz ripples provides specificity to the 80-120 Hz band.

results.result: Ripples detected in macro-scale iEEG occur simultaneously with ripples in micro-scale LFP across multiple microelectrodes and are accompanied by increases in spiking activity. The average spike rate is significantly correlated with both LFP ripple amplitude (r=0.751±0.188, p<0.05) and iEEG ripple amplitude (r=0.118±0.049, p=0.031) across participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by simultaneous recordings at multiple spatial scales (iEEG, LFP, and single units) in six participants. The correlations are statistically significant and consistent across participants, as shown in Figure 2. This multi-scale validation is a key strength of the study.

results.result: Ripples at both macro- and micro-scales exhibit a range of amplitudes and durations. Even ripples with amplitudes or durations below previously used thresholds are associated with spiking activity. The correlation between ripple amplitude and spike rate remains significant after accounting for ripple duration through shuffling procedures (LFP: true-shuffled r=0.096±0.020, p=0.011; iEEG: true-shuffled r=0.069±0.027, p=0.027).
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C44, C45, and C47 are supported by data showing a continuum of ripple characteristics and appropriate control analyses using shuffling procedures to account for potential confounds. The use of relaxed detection criteria and shuffling controls strengthens the conclusion that ripples exist on a spectrum.

results.result: The amplitude of iEEG ripples is positively correlated with the percentage of MEA electrodes exhibiting LFP ripples (r=0.11±0.02, p=0.005) and with the pairwise phase consistency (PPC) of LFP ripples (r=1.06±0.43, p=0.033). These correlations remain significant after accounting for ripple duration through shuffling procedures.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 demonstrate that macro-scale ripple amplitude reflects both the number and synchrony of micro-scale ripples. The use of shuffling controls to account for duration effects is appropriate, and the results are consistent across participants as shown in Figure 3.

results.result: Ripples are coincident above chance for all detection parameters tested. The extent of ripple coincidence between electrodes at different spatial scales is significantly related to the distance between them (all participants: r=-0.572, p=0.0035).
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C54 are supported by cross-correlation analyses shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures. The distance-dependent relationship provides additional evidence for the spatial organization of ripple activity.

results.result: Spikes are locked to the trough of 80-120 Hz ripples in the LFP signal (p<10⁻⁴) but not in the iEEG signal (p=0.12). Spikes are also locked to the trough of 2-10 Hz low-frequency activity in the LFP (p<10⁻⁴), but locking to the iEEG low-frequency signal is not consistent across participants (p=0.70).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by phase-locking analyses using Rayleigh tests, with results shown in Figure 4. The differential locking at micro- versus macro-scales is consistent with the interpretation that synchronous spiking can occur within local ensembles while varying across larger spatial scales.

results.result: Spiking activity is significantly locked to specific high-frequency bands in the LFP, with a peak at 86.9 Hz (p<0.05). Spikes are more locked to high frequencies during ripples compared to between ripples (p<0.05). The correlation between LFP ripple amplitude and spike locking to the 80-120 Hz band is significantly stronger in true data compared to shuffled data (p=0.023).
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, and C62 are supported by pairwise phase consistency analyses with appropriate permutation testing to correct for multiple comparisons. The results shown in Figure 4 demonstrate frequency-specific locking that is enhanced during ripples.

results.result: Micro-scale LFP ripples are locked to the trough of 2-10 Hz low-frequency activity in the LFP signal (p<10⁻⁴, p=0.0099 across participants). Ripples are also locked to low-frequency activity in the iEEG signal within individual participants but at variable phases (p<10⁻⁴ within participants, p=0.72 across participants).
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C64 are supported by phase-locking analyses of ripple events to low-frequency oscillations. The variable phase across participants for iEEG locking suggests that the relationship may reflect local sharp waves rather than consistent oscillatory coupling.

results.result: Cortical ripples exist on a continuum of amplitudes and durations, and even smaller ripples are associated with bursts of spiking activity. The amplitude and duration of micro-scale LFP ripples are related to the amount and synchrony of neuronal spiking, while macro-scale iEEG ripples are related to the number and synchrony of micro-scale ripples. The data argue against using fixed criteria to identify ripples.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70, C99, and C100 represent key interpretive conclusions that are well-supported by the multi-scale data. The use of relaxed detection criteria and demonstration of correlations across the full spectrum of ripple characteristics provide strong evidence for the continuum hypothesis.

results.result: The durations of ripples observed in human recordings are shorter than those observed in the rodent MTL, which could be related to differences in neural architecture between species or brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 makes a comparative statement about ripple durations across species, but the manuscript does not provide direct quantitative comparisons with rodent data. While the speculation about neural architecture differences is reasonable, it remains speculative without additional supporting evidence.

results.result: Fast oscillations within a narrow 80-120 Hz band were identified using multiple complementary analyses. These events are not related to epilepsy or interictal epileptiform discharges, are associated with MTL ripples, and are related to bursts of underlying spiking activity. The narrow band activity accounts for many changes in broadband power, and cortical spiking is locked to this band.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including MODAL detection (Figure 1—supplement 3), IED exclusion analyses (Figure 1—supplement 5), MTL-ATL cross-correlations (Figure 1—supplement 4), and phase-locking analyses (Figure 4). The convergence of multiple analytical approaches strengthens these conclusions.

results.result: The relation between 80-120 Hz ripples and broadband high-frequency activity is not absolute and appears less robust outside of the MTL and ATL. Even within these regions, the relation is clearer during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval. While ripples may underlie many phenomena observed through broadband HFA, other neural mechanisms likely contribute to iEEG dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the ripple-HFA relationship. These claims are supported by the regional specificity shown in Figure 1G and the behavioral modulation shown in Figure 1I. The acknowledgment of other contributing mechanisms is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: Neural activity in the human temporal cortex is temporally organized into discrete bursts of spiking. The results raise the possibility that packets of spiking activity may be a general feature of neural coding in the human brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C86 are supported by the direct evidence from microelectrode recordings showing bursts of spiking associated with ripples (Figure 2). However, the generalization to the entire human brain (C86) is appropriately framed as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion, given that data were collected only from the temporal lobe.

results.result: The data cannot address whether the relation between ripples and bursts of synchronized spiking is unique to the temporal lobe or to memory. It is possible that this relation is unique to brain regions that communicate with the MTL or are involved in memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C83 and C85 appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the study's scope. The data were collected only from the temporal lobe during a memory task, so these limitations are accurately stated.

results.result: Spiking activity within ripples is locked to the trough of each cycle, consistent with previous evidence. More consistent locking to higher frequencies is found at the micro- compared to macro-scale, which may be because synchronous spiking can occur within local neuronal ensembles while varying across ensembles.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by the phase-locking data in Figure 4B and are consistent with prior literature. The explanation for differential locking across spatial scales (C89) is speculative but reasonable given the data.

results.result: Spikes and ripples coincide with large deflections in the iEEG and LFP traces that have spectral power in low-frequency bands. This locking can account for phase-amplitude coupling between low-frequency oscillations and high-frequency activity. If broadband HFA is related to ripples, then phase-amplitude coupling may emerge because ripples coincide with sharp waves reflecting concentrated synaptic inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by the spike-triggered averages and phase-locking analyses shown in Figure 4C-D. The interpretation regarding phase-amplitude coupling is a reasonable inference from the data, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct PAC analyses.

results.result: Some locking between low-frequency power and spiking/ripples may reflect locking to true low-frequency oscillations, which could facilitate communication between brain regions. Two brain regions exhibiting bursts of spiking can each generate ripple oscillations that may appear coherent if underlying neuronal interactions are similar, or desynchronized if the architecture differs.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are largely speculative interpretations about mechanisms of inter-regional communication. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and prior literature, they are not directly tested in this study and should be considered as proposed mechanisms requiring future validation.

results.result: Ripple oscillations may constitute one of the primary substrates of human cognition.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 is a broad speculative conclusion that extends beyond the data presented. While the study provides strong evidence for ripples in the temporal lobe during memory tasks, the generalization to 'primary substrates of human cognition' is not directly supported by the data and represents a hypothesis for future investigation.

results.result: Participants studied 93±8 word pairs with 30.1±4.1% recall success. A total of 1660 iEEG electrodes (79±4 per participant) were recorded, with an average ripple rate of 0.35±0.04 Hz. In six participants with MEAs, 989 single units (72±21 per participant) were identified with mean spike rate 2.82±0.01 Hz. After preprocessing, 78±27 MEA electrodes were retained. Unit isolation quality was high (isolation score 0.93±0.1, SNR 1.71±0.12). IEDs overlapped with <2% of detected ripples.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C113 provide detailed methodological and descriptive statistics that are clearly reported and internally consistent. The quality metrics for single-unit recordings are appropriate and indicate good data quality.

results.result: The MODAL method detected events with mean duration 33.5±3.0 ms and center frequency 87.3±3.5 Hz, similar to the standard ripple detection approach (32.8±6.3 ms). Ripples are coincident across MTL and ATL regions above chance for all detection parameters tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 demonstrate that an independent detection method (MODAL) identifies similar events to the standard approach, providing methodological validation. The cross-regional coincidence analyses support the functional coupling of ripples across temporal lobe regions.

results.result: MEAs were implanted 14.6±3.7 mm away from the closest electrode with ictal or interictal activity. Four of six participants received surgical resection including the MEA implant site.
results.evaluation: Claims C118 and C119 provide important context about the clinical characteristics of the recording sites. The distance from epileptogenic tissue and the fact that most sites were subsequently resected are relevant for interpreting the data, though they also raise questions about the generalizability to non-pathological tissue.
